title: OIDC Authorization Code + PKCE
subtitle: The default flow for SPAs and native apps. Step through it and see what each request carries — and how to read it in the Network tab.

steps.label: User taps “Sign in”
steps.lede: The user starts sign-in in a public client (SPA or native app). Nothing has hit the network yet.
steps.devtools: Open DevTools (F12) → Network tab, enable Preserve log so redirects aren’t cleared, and filter on Doc / Fetch.

steps.label: Generate PKCE verifier + challenge
steps.lede: The client creates a random code_verifier and derives a code_challenge. The verifier never leaves the client until the token call.
steps.code:
code_verifier  = base64url(random(32 bytes))
             = "dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk"
code_challenge = base64url( SHA-256( code_verifier ) )
             = "E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM"
method         = S256
steps.devtools: Not a network event — but in a real app you can watch the verifier get stored in Session Storage (Application tab) before the redirect.

steps.label: Redirect to /authorize
steps.lede: The browser is redirected to the authorization endpoint. Note the challenge is sent, the verifier is not.
steps.devtools: Find the request to /authorize. Read the query string params — confirm code_challenge_method=S256 and that no secret is present. Copy state; you’ll match it on the way back.

steps.label: Login + consent screen
steps.lede: The IdP serves its login page (and consent, if required). Credentials are entered against the IdP, never the app.
steps.devtools: You’ll see the IdP’s own HTML documents and an idp_session cookie set with HttpOnly; Secure. Credentials post to the IdP’s domain — verify the origin is the real IdP.

steps.label: Redirect back with code
steps.lede: On success the IdP 302-redirects back to redirect_uri with a short-lived authorization code and the echoed state.
steps.devtools: Find the 302 whose Location header points at your redirect_uri. The code is in the query string. Verify the returned state equals the one you sent — a mismatch means CSRF; abort.

steps.label: Exchange code at /token
steps.lede: The client posts the code plus the original code_verifier. The IdP recomputes SHA-256(verifier) and checks it equals the stored challenge — this is what defeats a stolen code.
steps.devtools: Filter for token. Open the Payload tab: confirm code_verifier is present and there is no client_secret (public client). If this were a confidential client, the secret would be server-side and this call would not appear in the browser.

steps.label: Tokens returned
steps.lede: The IdP returns an access token, an ID token (a JWT about the user), and often a rotating refresh token.

jwt.title: Decoded id_token
payload: Must equal the nonce you sent in /authorize

steps.devtools: In the token response → Response tab, copy the id_token. It’s a JWT: three base64url parts split by .. Base64url-decode the first two for header and claims (or paste into jwt.io / use the Auth Inspector extension). Never trust a JWT you haven’t verified server-side.

steps.label: Call the API with the token
steps.lede: The client calls a resource server, presenting the access token as a Bearer credential.
steps.devtools: Find the API request and read the Authorization: Bearer request header. On the resource server this token is validated (signature via JWKS, iss, aud, exp, scopes) before the data is returned.

steps.label: Signed in
steps.lede: The client establishes its session from the validated tokens and shows the authenticated UI. The verifier, code, and any secrets are discarded.
steps.devtools: Nothing further on the wire for sign-in. A stolen authorization code from the redirect is now useless to an attacker: without the matching code_verifier, the token exchange fails with invalid_grant. That is PKCE.
